articles.text:
Fundraise Oct 30, 2026, 16:30 UTC
AI agent security startup AIR raises $50M seed, lands on Fortune Cyber 60
What's the deal? AIR Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → , a Tel Aviv-based startup securing enterprise AI agents, was named to Fortune's 2026–2027 Cyber 60 list after raising $50 million across two seed rounds. Sequoia led a $10 million round and Greenoaks led a $40 million round.
What does it build? AIR sells a security layer for AI agents and the ecosystem of add-ons that extend them — skills, plugins, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. The platform continuously vets those components, enforces policies at runtime, and offers a marketplace of pre-vetted add-ons.
Why now? Enterprises adopting AI agents are inheriting fresh risk from the tools those agents access, which can change over time. AIR frames the problem as a supply chain issue rather than one of model access or prompt filtering.
"Approving an AI add-on once isn't enough," said Yair Saban, co-founder and chief executive officer of AIR. "Organizations need to know what their agents are using, whether those components remain trustworthy, and when to revoke access."
About the list. Fortune produced the Cyber 60 with Lightspeed Venture Partners and AWS , recognizing 60 venture-backed cybersecurity startups across three stages of growth. AIR emerged from stealth in September.
What could go wrong? List inclusion is third-party validation, not proof of commercial traction. The open question is whether AIR can convert investor interest into enterprise adoption in a crowded, fast-moving market.
The signal: A $50 million seed is unusually large for a cybersecurity startup, and it reflects where capital is flowing.

articles.text:
Knowledge Hub Press Release October 27, 2026

Hyphenate raises $45M Series A following 86x revenue growth as CFOs move to autonomous finance
October 27, 2026 6 min read
Hyphenate’s customer base grew 11x in 12 months, including six public companies, and its self-learning agents now run 90% of routine finance work across the platform.
Summarize With: Open in ChatGPT Open in Claude Open in Grok
Share Link Book a Call
New York City, NY - October 27, 2026 ; The first wave of finance AI helped teams work faster. The next is taking responsibility for the work itself. Hyphenate , the autonomous finance platform for the office of the CFO, today announced a $45 million Series A led by Nexus Venture Partners, with participation from B Capital and existing investors including Foundation Capital, BoldCap and Gaia Ventures.
Inside Hyphenate customers, agents are already reconciling cash, processing sales orders, running invoicing, maintaining subledgers and moving the close forward, with finance teams stepping in only where judgment changes the outcome. The round, which brings total funding to $54 million, comes less than a month after Maximor rebranded to Hyphenate, as customers expand its use across the office of the CFO. The company will use the capital to take its agents deeper across the finance function and into strategic finance.
“Every finance team carries a long list of work it does because somebody has to,” said Ramnandan Krishnamurthy, co-founder and CEO of Hyphenate . “Our customers are watching that list shrink in production. Once a team sees the system handle one workflow to an auditor’s standard, they hand it the next one. That is the pattern this company is built around, and this round lets us run it across the whole function.”
12 months from seed to 86x
Hyphenate raised a $9 million seed one year ago to take repetitive work off finance teams. Since then, the company has passed multi-million-dollar ARR, its agents have taken on work across hundreds of entities, thousands of bank accounts and millions of transactions every day, and customers report 90% less repetitive finance work and 75% fewer audit exceptions. The more telling number is what customers do next: 40% expand within their first year, several by two to three times, and the average customer runs six modules.Companies are handing the system larger parts of finance once it has proved itself in one workflow.
What that looks like in production
The expansion is now visible in production, at companies where finance errors carry real cost.
Mini Melts USA, the consumer goods company, runs Hyphenate agents on top of its SAP environment for orders, invoicing and refunds. Within three months of going live, the company was getting back 16,640 hours of finance work a year.
HiBid, one of the largest online auction platforms in North America, has run more than $2.5 billion in GMV through full order-to-cash automation on Hyphenate. Invoicing, collections and cash application across that volume now run as a single continuous process, and the company has cut its month-end close from three weeks to one day.
Groupon, the Nasdaq-listed marketplace, is replacing legacy and home-grown systems with Hyphenate across treasury, order-to-cash and more than a dozen subledger processes.

articles.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
articles.snippet: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache TechCrunch
articles.text:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.
Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.
That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.
When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.
“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”
Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.
“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.
In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.
